title: ElasticMM: Efficient Multimodal LLMs Serving with Elastic Multimodal Paral

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract vs. Introduction, Conclusion, and Evaluation
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract states 'reducing TTFT by up to 6.8× and achieving 5.1–7.2× higher throughput', but the introduction (end of Section 1) says 'reduces TTFT by up to 4.2× and achieves a 3.2×–4.5× throughput improvement'. The conclusion repeats 'up to 4.2× reduction in TTFT and 3.2–4.5× higher throughput compared to vLLM'. The experimental results in Section 4.2 show a maximum TTFT reduction of 4.2× and maximum throughput improvement of 4.5× over vLLM. The abstract's numbers are unsupported and contradict the rest of the paper.

Llama-3.2 Vision is described as an encoder-decoder architecture and cited as [21] (also in Table 1). Reference [21] is 'J. Chi et al., Llama Guard 3 Vision: Safeguarding human-AI image understanding conversations', which is a safety-classifier model, not the Llama 3.2 Vision multimodal model. The correct reference for Llama 3.2 Vision is not [21]; this misattributes the architecture claim.

The text states 'Zhang et al. [61] proposed a similar two-tier separation in 2024 but lacked elastic scheduling.' No reference [61] exists in the bibliography; the reference list ends at [60]. This is a missing/fabricated citation.

The text says 'Burst tolerance (bt) is defined as the difference between peak load and idle capacity normalized by total instances, as formalized in Equation 1.' Equation (1) gives bt(i) = N_i^{peak} / N_i^{avg}, which is a ratio of instance counts, not a difference normalized by total instances. The definition in words is inconsistent with the formula.

The proof states: 'For data parallelism with n devices: g_E^{DP_n}(i) = Gather({g_E^1(i_1), g_E^2(i_2), ..., g_E^n(i_n)}) where i_1, i_2, ..., i_n represent partitions of input i'. Image encoders (e.g., ViT) do not work by partitioning a single image into pieces and encoding each piece separately on different devices, then gathering. Data parallelism for encoding processes multiple images (or batches) in parallel, not partitions of one image. The described parallelism is incorrect and undermines the claimed invariance.
